title: 49 minutes of terror and tragedy in Toronto
article: It was rush hour and a young police constable, working a pay-duty shift outside the Royal York Hotel, spotted 45-year-old Sugston Anthony Brookes just minutes before he would grab a young woman and hold a gun to her head.

The officer confronted him because he matched the description coming across his police radio of a man who had fired shots in a food court in the middle of Toronto's financial district, Toronto Police Chief Julian Fantino said.
Mr. Brookes fled, crossing Front Street and heading west. The officer, by now with backup on the way, followed him, staying across the street. Minutes later, Mr. Brookes grabbed his hostage.
Police officers from at least four different divisions rushed to the scene, running along Front Street.
They ushered bewildered commuters out of the area. Officers were soon crouched behind garbage cans, taxicabs, police cruisers and lampposts around the hostage-taker, their handguns drawn.
The force's heavily armed emergency task force tactical squad also arrived, staking out positions and pointing high-powered rifles at Mr. Brookes.
Police, one of them a specially trained ETF negotiator, tried twice to negotiate with Mr. Brookes, Chief Fantino said.

"Efforts to negotiate or elicit a response from the suspect did not work out," Chief Fantino told reporters at the scene yesterday morning. "His movements were threatening all along, brandishing the firearm at officers and at the woman."

The hostage, a handbag over her shoulder, spent much of the time looking down, her hands folded in front of her. Mr. Brookes appeared to speak to her, often moving from side to side, constantly watching police movement around him.

With normally bustling Front Street now shut down and eerily silent, one booming shot, fired by an ETF officer, rang out at about 8:50 a.m., striking Mr. Brookes in the head. Both he and his hostage fell to the ground.
After a moment, the hostage ran off into the arms of police and ambulance staff, while Mr. Brookes lay in a large pool of blood.
The hostage, believed to be 19 or 20, was identified by CTV News as Nicole Regis.
A summer student at the Royal Bank, she was described as "engaging and popular" by a co-worker who spoke on condition of anonymity. Yesterday was her last day of work.
Ms. Regis is reportedly the daughter of Ontario Court Judge Gregory Regis, who could not be reached for comment at his Ajax, Ont., home yesterday.
The province's Special Investigations Unit, which probes police incidents that result in serious injury or death, has designated two subject officers in the shooting and 17 witness officers.
"There was no choice," Chief Fantino said yesterday. "I feel the officers did what they had to, what they were trained to do."
Police knew that the man had already fired shots just after 8 a.m., missing his estranged wife and then assaulting her at a food court underneath the nearby TD Centre.

After hearing those first gunshots, Eli Shimonov, a former Israeli paratrooper and the owner of Pumpernickel's Deli in the food court, ushered customers, staff and his wife and children into the large walk-in fridge at the back of the restaurant.

He then ventured into the empty food court to assist the woman, who was lying on the ground, bleeding heavily from a head wound. She was taken to St. Michael's Hospital, received a few stitches to her head and was in stable condition last night.
About an hour after that first attack, Mr. Brookes was dead at the hands of a police sharpshooter.
"The left side of his brain just, like, flew into the air," said Anna Boublikova, 21, a bank teller on her third day on the job in the TD Centre.
She was in a car on Front Street when Mr. Brookes ran across the street. Police told her to take shelter in the hotel. They went up to the third floor and watched from a window.
Donna Dunn, an administrative assistant on her way to work, passed the gunman as he crossed Front Street some time after 8 a.m.
She said a police officer walking towards her from the Royal York Hotel shouted, "Drop the gun!" The officer was running towards them, gun drawn, talking into a walkie-talkie, she said.

The man, who walked quickly but didn't run, then calmly approached a woman standing nearby and grabbed her around the throat. "I looked up to see a cop with his gun pointed in our direction and I dove for a car. I just dove," she said. "I'll never forget seeing his face."
She said the officer yelled forcefully at first, but then more gently, asking the man to drop the weapon.
Ms. Dunn stayed hidden behind the car for five minutes, and even called her boss to warn him she'd be late for work. She later retreated across Front Street as police arrived to clear the scene.
Premier Dalton McGuinty expressed a "sense of relief that the hostage is safe and has emerged from what must have been a very traumatic incident unharmed."
The emergency task force was formed in 1966, and its highly trained officers had used deadly force fewer than 10 times before yesterday's incident.

From 1979 to 1991, the heavily armed ETF didn't kill one suspect, despite responding to 2,000 emergencies involving barricaded suspects and hostage-takers. The force's ETF handles more than 400 calls a year involving people armed with some kind of a weapon.

"I said, 'Oh, they're shooting a movie,' because I saw the police with their guns drawn. Then I said, 'Wait a minute; there's too many extras for a movie shoot.' " -- Dena Castro walked out of Union Station in the middle of the hostage-taking.
"He was standing there with his arm around her. He had completely blocked her, and you could see her feet moving back and forth.

"It's what happens in television and not in real life. The whole idea of this is awful. It's just what Toronto has become lately: gun crazy." -- Susan Cormier was standing at a bank machine in Union Station.

"It wasn't sudden. It was very slow. He stood next to her for a second, and then he grabbed her. She was crying, I believe, in the beginning, and then she just covered her face and stood there quietly.
"He just took a step back for like a second, and that second they shot him. Right there." -- Oroosh Sheikh was waiting in a car on Front Street.

"I was shaking when I went up to my room. I heard chaos and gunfire. It was just one big boom." -- George Desousa was walking outside the Royal York, where he was staying as a guest. "We were watching them trying to negotiate with him. We didn't know what they were saying, but the guy was holding the gun to her head pretty close. Snipers all over the place. It was pretty quick. Then boom -- see him get shot in the head. Everything was all over the place.
"When I saw the bullet go through his head, I was shaking." -- Muz Jaffer was in a car on Front Street.

"Obviously there was a very serious situation, and they have to make that decision [to shoot] That was their decision, and I'm not prepared to second-guess them." -- Ontario Community Safety Minister Monte Kwinter.
